Everyone’s read this one as complete proof AI agents can’t be trusted.
I think that’s almost a lazy version 👀

Someone asked their agent to book them into a popular morning gym class. It found a flaw that let it book further ahead than the gym allows. They were fourth on a waitlist so they asked whether it could get them higher up. It cancelled the booking of the person sitting at number one. Nobody asked it to do that. It worked out it could & so it did.
They told it to undo. It couldn’t.

The reason is the whole story. The gym’s software checked authorisation properly on creating a booking & on joining a waitlist. Try either on someone else’s behalf & you get a 403. It never checked authorisation on cancelling. So an agent could delete a stranger but not restore them.
Someone lost their spot & was never told why.

That gap was built by a developer who thought carefully about who could take something & never about who could lose something. It sat there long before any agent found it. What the agent changed is how fast somebody walked into it.
So the useful question isn’t whether we trust agents. It’s what our systems already let anything holding valid credentials do & whether we can reverse it when it does.
Most teams I sit with can answer the first half. Almost nobody has tested the second.
Happy because I made my early class that wasn’t cancelled and a 65kg double lift that made me question life choices 😂

This statement is so so dangerous.
“Don’t bother studying law. AI will take your career.”
A throwaway statement by the founder of Google’s Generative AI team in a recent article.
Yes, people are allowed to have opinions.
But is this really an opinion or just scaremongering?
For a profession that will need new talent entering the market at some point, this is one sure way to kill it.
And that won’t be because of AI.
It will be because of people not thinking about the impact of their words.
It frustrates me massively.
Students DO NOT need to hear this.
Yes, they do need to understand how AI will and is impacting their sector, massively.
No one is arguing against that.
But surely, we should be helping them.
Surely, we should be sharing knowledge, insights, and ways they can prepare, instead of leaving them with fear and ignorance.
The lawyers who will succeed will know how to bring together AI, human insight, and real-world judgment.
Success will come from building connections, not just completing tasks:
- Making complex information understandable and useful
- Linking the law to business, technology, ethics, and human behavior
- Using tools and tech to enhance their judgment, not replace it
AI isn’t going to destroy legal careers. What it is doing is restructuring them.
Legal information is everywhere, searchable, instant, overwhelming.
Knowledge won’t be power anymore. But that’s not the problem.
The problem, and the opportunity, is trust. Lawyers still matter because in a world drowning in information, clarity, judgment, and credibility are what will matter.
The role of a lawyer isn’t disappearing.
The law degree isn’t worthless.
The game however is changing and that’s exactly why it’s exciting.
This is exactly why I am passionate about educating, spend time mentoring law students & launched a free student community within my Knowledge Nexus platform this year.
It’s why I’ve led multiple guest lectures at Middlesex University Dubai on AI & Legal Tech to empower students to learn how the industry is changing.
Debate is important.
Fear-mongering and sweeping judgments aren’t.
And they don’t actually help anyone in the legal sector.
Why can’t we focus preparing the next generation, not frightening them?

About
Bridging the gap between legal expertise, technology and operational change with over 20 years of experience in legal tech consulting, strategy and legal operations.

I work with law firms, in-house legal teams, legal tech companies and corporates globally, with a strong focus on the Middle East, helping teams better understand how AI, legal technology and process improvement can genuinely support the business.

Having worked within leading legal tech companies responsible for millions in technology sales and client engagement, I understand not just the tools themselves, but the workflows, stakeholder challenges and business mindset needed for successful adoption.

I work with legal teams at different stages of AI and legal tech maturity, from those starting to explore strategy and workflows, to teams that have already adopted technology but are struggling with adoption, process alignment, stakeholder buy-in or maximising the value of the tools they already have in place.

Many teams don’t actually start with a technology problem. They start with workflow inefficiencies, fragmented communication, lack of visibility, unclear processes or pressure from the business to “do something with AI” without a clear strategy behind it.

My role is to work alongside legal teams to map out workflows, identify operational pain points, understand stakeholder needs and assess where technology, AI and process redesign can genuinely add value before tools are selected or implemented.
That vendor-neutral, people-and-process-first approach helps teams make better long-term technology decisions and improves adoption across the business.

My work spans AI strategy, legal operations, workflow design, legal intake, contracting, investigations, litigation support, compliance, M&A and digital transformation projects. I’ve supported teams including Americana, E&, Dubizzle and QatarEnergy.
I specialise in:
• AI & Legal Tech Strategy
• Legal Operations & Workflow Optimisation
• Technology Adoption & Stakeholder Buy-In
• Legal Workflow & Intake Transformation
• Go-to-Market Strategy for Legal Tech Companies
• Training, Workshops & Education

Alongside consulting, I’m also the MD & leading Knowledge Nexus, a legal education and community platform focused on AI, legal tech, legal operations and the future of work. Through accredited training, events and global communities, I’m passionate about helping legal professionals and the next generation build practical, ethical and commercially valuable technology skills.

Read recently that Anthropic has hired a Head of Claude for Legal.

Takes me back to chats with lawyers in the last week even. How many lawyers the big tools are hiring now & it isn’t only the legal tech companies doing it, the model makers are as well. Bringing people in to work on the workflows & the reasoning & how a matter actually gets handled.
I’ve seen job posts for things like IP lawyer experts and more for Claude and others.
Consensus is that the tools are still being fine tuned but there isn’t time to sit & just wait for them to be finished, which I agree with, but it’s only half of what’s going on.
The bigger issue is that most teams still treat adoption like a project with an end date, so you pick something, train everyone & roll it out & move on.

It doesn’t work like that. A few months in you’ve got people using it for things nobody planned for, workflows that need rebuilding because they were designed around what the tool couldn’t do yet, & a handful of new starters who were never in the room for the training.
None of that means it’s gone wrong, it’s just what this actually looks like.

Which is why the hire is interesting. He’s said the expertise that matters sits with practitioners & that this is being co-designed with the legal community, so he’s telling you fairly plainly that it isn’t finished & won’t be. That what gets built comes from how your people actually work.
Interesting times for legal and tech ✨
Going to miss being able to walk around in sunshine not needing a shower for a few weeks…

I walked past my very first office yesterday!
Where a very young (two whole decades 👀) me started out in M&A.
Roll forward to this week.
Tube strikes, Cancelled trains
Classic London weather (sun, rain, coat, sunglasses, all in one day)
Back then I was on the 5:30am train to Liverpool Street.
Long days.
Overnighters.
M&A deals that didn’t stop at 2am when you were running the tech alongside lawyers.
Those years shaped everything.
Learning what lawyers need before they know it themselves.
Figuring out the problem just by listening.
And it didn’t happen overnight.
AI or no AI, lawyers will still need that journey of learning.
Which is why I think the “AI will take all our jobs” narrative is wrong.
Change is needed, yes.
But it’s about education:
Real stories
Failures as much as successes
Knowing what works (and what doesn’t)
It’s why lawyers come to me almost daily asking:
“Where do I start?”
“I know we have a problem, but how do we fix it?”
The answer always comes back to the same thing.
Education.
People.
And that never stops.

If I’m ever in London and you want to catch up you will find me in the Ned 👀
Because it has and always has been about people & connection ☺️

Let’s talk remote work freedom fantasies…
Freedom without structure quickly turns into chaos
Remote work isn’t just about Wi-Fi and a laptop.
It’s about building habits and finding spaces that actually work for you.
Here’s what I’ve learned working for myself (and often on the move 🌍
🔹 Change your scenery - Not everything needs silence. For deep focus & client calls, I stay home.
If I’m flagging, I’ll head to a co-working space or café, just enough atmosphere to feel part of the buzz and that I’m not alone.

🔹Build a routine that works for you - just because I don’t have to rush to an office doesn’t mean I skip structure. For me, morning gym creates this, sets my energy for the day and most importantly surrounds me with people.
Especially important if I am at the laptop alone all day!

🔹 Take resets - When I feel stuck, I don’t push through. Sometimes it’s a quick walk (or run 👀). Sometimes it’s moving locations. Other times, it’s finding a place that truly relaxes me so I can shut the laptop completely.
I know im fortunate, for me, that often means a place with a sea view, which is for me calmness.
🔹 Protect your peak hours. Mornings for strategy & creativity, afternoons for calls for me but find what works for you!
🔹 Create a SEPARATE work space at home. I’m talking proper desk set up that you can walk away from.
Sofa working sounds dreamy until you can’t separate work from everything else and get brain fog.
🔹 Mix people back in. Working for yourself can be incredibly isolating. Book coffee catch-ups, drop into a networking breakfast, or work somewhere with a bit of buzz.
Grab a friend who’s also remote for a cafe laptop day..
Remote work is freedom
But it only works if you design it with intention.
Whilst everyone else parties in Marbella I’ve been hunting down the best laptop cafe stops for a change of scenery 👀
Can you spot the one I saw someone ordering a sangria whilst having that reset break 👀
👉 What’s your go to hack that keeps you sane + productive working remote?
PS…. London folks, ill be in town next week and organising a Thursday morning Hyde Park run if anyone wants to join me?

I get asked which tool to buy all the time. Almost nobody asks who they’re buying it from.

I talk a lot about shiny tools & sorting your data out first, because bad in, bad out. Both still stand, but who you're actually buying from gets far less airtime. Every provider will tell you they're a partner & most of them mean it.

An F1 car is extraordinary engineering right up until you get in and realise you don't know how to drive it. Legal tech is pretty much the same. The technology matters but it rarely decides whether it works.
The questions I'd ask anyone before signing:
Who will you actually be dealing with in month three, not the sales team?
Is there someone to call who understands legal workflows, not just password resets?
Will they help you build a playbook? AI in contracting is only as good as your clause library.
What's the plan for the first ninety days? A vendor will describe implementation, a partner will describe what happens after it.
Chatting to Alexandria (Lexi) Lutz, GC at contract intelligence system Summize, about exactly this at London’s LegalTechTalk!

As a GC she's been on the buying side too. "No in-house team I know started with a playbook. The partner helped us build ours, the vendor sent a template. And after go-live I needed numbers for the board, not anecdotes." Their clients say the same. One team of two said "We're just two people and we need a super strong support partnership", that's the reality for so many in-house teams. It's why who you can call matters more than the demo.
The other one is whether it properly sits inside the everyday tools your team already lives in, not 3 million buttons to get there...

Another GC, another legal team. They'd bought a contract and matter management tool for efficiency, oversight and, above all, reporting, so they could finally show the business what legal was doing. On paper it was fine. Yet hardly anyone used it, and they couldn't work out why.

I asked them to show me their day to day, and it clicked. It didn't connect to anything they worked in, so every email, matter and contract had to be entered by hand. A tool bought to save lawyers time was asking them for data entry. That isn't a training problem. It's a blocker, and no amount of encouragement fixes it.
The lesson for anyone buying, ask how it fits the way your team already works before you ask what it can do!

Oct 26
A demo shows you the product. A trial shows you the fit 👀
Sophie Best has seen similar patterns with clients again and again. A shiny tool looks perfect in the demo, then can struggle once it meets the team’s real work
The complex contracts, the existing systems, the way people actually draft, review and sign off.
Nobody tested that properly, because the evaluation stopped at the demo.

A proper trial is a simulation of how your team really works, run on your hardest tasks by the lawyers who will use the tool every day. Map five use cases as they work today and ask the vendor to set each one up. Check it works inside the systems you already use. Then ask the governance questions before you sign, not after.
Go live is the start, not the finish.
Who will own it after launch? Who will run training and change management?

Let’s talk conference exhaustion 👀
You pretty much are switched on constantly. The smile doesn’t leave.

Rushing to the bathroom, stopped on the way but too polite so you stop and have the conversation. After all I have immense appreciation for people who step out their comfort zone here and actually try to interact.
I know some of you hover at the back but that gets zero connection 😉
Then add in flights even short ones like DXB to Kuwait. Hanging around airports. All the waiting.

I’ll forever be grateful for firms granting me the space to talk at these. Especially when it’s things I’m so passionate about. The future of legal. How we can responsibly roll out tech & AI. No doom & gloom just how to approach it and move forward.
But these days I also 💯look after my mental health. Something I never would have done whilst in corporate or junior.
So yesterday after a fantastic two days and 30 minutes before the airport pick up I shut the laptop and headed to the spa. Anyone who knows Jumeirah hotels will know Talise is the creme de la creme!

I’ve said it before and I’ll shout it always. Lawyers need to pause to perform (stolen from my favourite meditation girly Melissa Gray) Exhaustion & burnout is real. And in the words of my favourite Doctor Shefali Verma, control those controllables 😉
The emails can wait. After all what difference is 30 minutes in ‘most’ situations. You go back more refreshed and ready to take the day back.
Keep your eyes peeled for two of my famous The Wellness Brief for Lawyers events coming soon 👀

Let’s talk remote work freedom fantasies…

Freedom without structure quickly turns into chaos

Remote work isn’t just about Wi-Fi and a laptop.
It’s about building habits and finding spaces that actually work for you.

Here’s what I’ve learned working for myself (and often on the move 🌍

🔹 Change your scenery - Not everything needs silence. For deep focus & client calls, I stay home.
If I’m flagging, I’ll head to a co-working space or café, just enough atmosphere to feel part of the buzz and that I’m not alone.

🔹Build a routine that works for you - just because I don’t have to rush to an office doesn’t mean I skip structure. For me, morning gym creates this, sets my energy for the day and most importantly surrounds me with people. 

Especially important if I am at the laptop alone all day!

🔹 Take resets - When I feel stuck, I don’t push through. Sometimes it’s a quick walk (or run 👀). Sometimes it’s moving locations. Other times, it’s finding a place that truly relaxes me so I can shut the laptop completely.

I know im fortunate, for me, that often means a place with a sea view, which is for me calmness.

🔹 Protect your peak hours. Mornings for strategy & creativity, afternoons for calls for me but find what works for you!

🔹 Create a SEPARATE work space at home. I’m talking proper desk set up that you can walk away from. 

Sofa working sounds dreamy until you can’t separate work from everything else and get brain fog.

🔹 Mix people back in. Working for yourself can be incredibly isolating. Book coffee catch-ups, drop into a networking breakfast, or work somewhere with a bit of buzz. 

Grab a friend who’s also remote for a cafe laptop day..

Remote work is freedom
But it only works if you design it with intention.

This statement is so so dangerous.
“Don’t bother studying law. AI will take your career.”

A throwaway statement by the founder of Google’s Generative AI team in a recent article.

Yes, people are allowed to have opinions. 
But is this really an opinion or just scaremongering?

For a profession that will need new talent entering the market at some point, this is one sure way to kill it. 

And that won’t be because of AI.
It will be because of people not thinking about the impact of their words.

It frustrates me massively.
Students DO NOT need to hear this.

Yes, they do need to understand how AI will and is impacting their sector, massively. 
No one is arguing against that. 

But surely, we should be helping them. 
Surely, we should be sharing knowledge, insights, and ways they can prepare, instead of leaving them with fear and ignorance.

The lawyers who will succeed will know how to bring together AI, human insight, and real-world judgment.

Success will come from building connections, not just completing tasks:

- Making complex information understandable and useful
- Linking the law to business, technology, ethics, and human behavior
- Using tools and tech to enhance their judgment, not replace it

AI isn’t going to destroy legal careers. What it is doing is restructuring them. 

Legal information is everywhere, searchable, instant, overwhelming. 

Knowledge won’t be power anymore. But that’s not the problem.

The problem, and the opportunity, is trust. Lawyers still matter because in a world drowning in information, clarity, judgment, and credibility are what will matter.

The role of a lawyer isn’t disappearing. 
The law degree isn’t worthless. 
The game however is changing and that’s exactly why it’s exciting.

This is exactly why I am passionate about educating, spend time mentoring law students & launched a free student community within my Knowledge Nexus platform this year.

It’s why I’ve led multiple guest lectures at Middlesex University Dubai on AI & Legal Tech to empower students to learn how the industry is changing.

Debate is important. 
Fear-mongering and sweeping judgments aren’t.
And they don’t actually help anyone in the legal sector.

Why can’t we focus preparing the next generation, not frightening them?
